summary.text: Taking the quantified value \(n=0\), all terms in the defining expression vanish, so \(a(0)=0\). But \(0\) is neither \(1\) nor prime, contradicting the asserted characterization of the zeros.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
D(n)=\{d\in\mathbb N:1\le d<n+1\text{ and }d\mid n\}.
\]
Thus, for positive \(n\), \(D(n)\) is the usual finite set of positive divisors of \(n\). Define
\[
\sigma_1(n)=\sum_{d\in D(n)}d,
\qquad
\sigma_2(n)=\sum_{d\in D(n)}d^2,
\]
and let \(\varphi(n)\) be Euler's totient, extended at zero by the convention \(\varphi(0)=0\). The version of the sequence used in the statement is the natural-number value obtained from
\[
E(n)=\sigma_2(n)+\varphi(n)\sigma_1(n)-2n^2
\]
by replacing a negative integer by \(0\); in other words,
\[
a(n)=\max(E(n),0).
\]
(The truncation is immaterial in the counterexample below because \(E(0)=0\).)

The statement asserted for every natural number \(n\), with no hypothesis \(n\ge 1\), that both
\[
a(n)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n=1\text{ or }n\text{ is prime}
\tag{1}
\]
and
\[
a(n)=2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n=pq\text{ for two distinct primes }p,q
\tag{2}
\]
hold. We disprove this universal statement by taking \(n=0\).

First compute the divisor sums at zero according to the displayed definition of \(D(n)\). An element of \(D(0)\) would have to satisfy
\[
1\le d<0+1=1,
\]
which is impossible. Hence
\[
D(0)=\varnothing.
\]
Both sums over this empty set therefore vanish:
\[
\sigma_1(0)=0,
\qquad
\sigma_2(0)=0.
\]
Together with \(\varphi(0)=0\) and \(0^2=0\), this gives
\[
E(0)
 =\sigma_2(0)+\varphi(0)\sigma_1(0)-2\cdot0^2
 =0+0\cdot0-0
 =0.
\]
Consequently
\[
a(0)=\max(E(0),0)=0.
\tag{3}
\]

Now apply the claimed equivalence (1) at \(n=0\). By (3), its left-hand side is true, so its right-hand side would force the disjunction
\[
0=1\quad\text{or}\quad 0\text{ is prime}.
\tag{4}
\]
There are two cases, and each is impossible. In the first case, \(0=1\), contradicting the distinctness of zero and one. In the second case, \(0\) is prime, contradicting the defining fact that a prime natural number is at least \(2\) (equivalently, \(0\) is not prime). Thus (4) is false. It follows that equivalence (1) fails at \(n=0\). Since the asserted statement was a conjunction of (1) and (2) for every natural number, failure of its first conjunct at this single value is enough to disprove the entire universal statement; no analysis of (2) is needed.

Therefore the statement quantified over all \(n\in\mathbb N\) is false.

There is an important domain qualification. The OEIS conjecture as ordinarily worded says “for every \(n\ge1\).” The counterexample \(n=0\) does not satisfy that hypothesis. Accordingly, this argument disproves the accepted formal statement, which omitted the condition \(n\ge1\); it does not by itself disprove the positive-index conjecture in the canonical description.
